Canto II

Now o'er the cedar forest ruddy morn
Descended. The divine Redeemer rose.
When in the sun the patriarchal souls
Beheld him, thus the happy souls of Eve
And Adam sung alternate. First our Sire.
Hail, Blessed Day, most blissful of the days,
That are yet in futurity reserved!
Before the train of thy companions, thou
Shalt ever be most sacred, most belov'd!
Seraph and Cherub with the human soul,
Shall ever hail, with loud acclaims of joy
And festal song, thy hallowed return.
Or to the earth descending, or announced
By lofty' Orion through celestial realms;
Or whether coming forth from thy recess,
Advancing radiant by the Throne of God
We still with festal splendour will receive,
And bless thy rising and declining light:
We e'er will celebrate, Immortal Day,
Thee jubilant, with shouts and hallelujahs.
Thou art the day on which our eyes consol'd,
The first time saw in his humility
The blessed Mediator, the divine
Messiah, e'en our God in human form.
Thou, who didst bring the great Messiah forth,
Blessed art thou and holy, blessed more
Than Eve, the parent of the human race.
Eve is the parent of a countless race,
A countless race of sinners. Thou hast born
Anionly son, — he is a righteous man,
Is pure, is holy, is immaculate,
Is the Messiah, an Eternal Son,
Divine and Self-existent. — Down to th' earth
With roving eye affectionate I gaze,
Bat cannot now my paradise discern.
Oh, Blissful Garden, the restless. floods
Have with the dreadful judgment swept thee hence!
Thy lofty cedars, planted by the hand
Divine; thy peaceful arbours, the abode
Of juvenile virtues; none of you escap'd
The desolation dire of thundering tempests,
And the destroying Angel's awful sword!
But thou, O Bethlehem, where Mary brought him forth;
Where with maternal ecstasy she first
Embraced him; thou my Eden art henceforth.
And thou, O Well of David, thou shalt be
To me the lake, where.coming from the hands
Of my Creator, I first saw myself.
Thou humble Cot, where first he wept, be thou
To me th' umbrageous bower of innocence.
Primeval! — Oh, If I had brought Thee forth,
In Eden, Thou Divine Messiah, after
The hideous deed of sin; Behold, I would
Have borne Thee in mine arms before my Jude;
E'en where he stood, where Eden under him
Became a yawning grave; there, v where the tree
Of knowledge shook terrific; where the Judge
Spake out of tempest and pronounced my fate
Where I was lost in terror and affright,
And trembling sunk to faint and die away;
E'en there I would have looked up to my Judge,
And weeping would, have clasped Thee in mine arm?,
And pressed Thee closer to my throbbing; heart,
And would with ecstasy have cried aloud;
O Father, cease to frown; from anger cease!
Behold, I have brought forth the dear (Messiah.
Eternal, holy, adorable First Cause!
In mercy Thou gavest thine -Eternal Sen,
My ruined progeny from, death to save
My tears hate often flowed on. %irbthal&
Nor could the high felicity of heav'n
Have' cheered my drooping, my lamenting soul,
Had the Divine Messiah not resolv'd,
My children from destruction to redeem.
Bat Thou, who in compassion didst decree
Th' eternal covenant, Thou, all-gracious, has
Enabled me still to derive new bliss
E'en from paternal sadness and dolour.
And now, Divine, adorable Redeemer,
Thou even bear'st man's image! O complete
The sacrifice which, Dread Judge of the world,
Thou hast resolved to bring for us to th' altar.
Renew the beauty of our native earth,
Which purpose to effect Thou dust descend,
And then return, O come, with speed return
To heavenly realms! We wilt, God, Mediator,
Hail thy return with festal hallelujahs.
The voices of these fervent souls with pow'r
Resounded thus through the refulgent domes
Of sanctuary and temple. And remote
The Saviour heard them as in solitude
The Sage perceives, in contemplation wrapp'd,
Prophetic whispers of th' Eternal's voice.
The Saviour now from Olivet came down.
Below the hoary mountain's lofty bights
Small eminences raised a grove of palm,
Still with the fleeting dew of morning deck'd.
And in the tufted palm -grove Jesus saw
John's Guardian Angel, (Raphael is his name,)
Who worshipped the Messiah on his knees.
Still breezes wafted to the Mediator

Come Raphael, answered Jesus with benign
And friendly mien; draw nearer to my side.
Attend me unobserved. How didst thou guard
Beneath the shades of night in these lone haunts,
The pious soul of my beloved Disciple,
E'en John? how did his thoughts with thine accord?
Where hast thou left him? und where is he now?
I guarded him, Adorable Redeemer,
So as we guard the Firstlings of thy flock.
And sacred dreams, e'en dreams of Thee, his mind
Surrounded while he lay in slumber wrapped.
Oh that Thou hadst observed him when he dream'd
That Thou, Messiah, didst tow'rd him advance;
How o'er his countenance soft vernal smiles suffuzM!
Thy Seraph saw, e'en in the blissful fields
Of Eden, Adam; when he in his sleep
Beheld the beauteous imago of his Eve,
And saw the Great Creator's forming hand.
But. scarcely were his smiles so full of love
And holy rapture, as thy sacred presence
DuTuzed o'er the countenance of John.
But now he is among the gloomy' and drear
Receptacles of the dead, lamenting there
Over a poor Demoniac who, with pale
Distorted visage, trembles in the dust.
0 come, Divine Redeemer, him to see!
See bow His tender heart in grief dissolves;
See how he stands and trembles with concern.
Myself could not avoid a tear to shed
Of tender sympathy. I withdrew. Thou know'at,
1 never could the painful sight sustain,
Of Spirits thus distress'd, whom Thou createdst
To live for ever and in happy state.
Thus, Raphael ceased. The Saviour looked to heav'n,
And, indignation darting from his eyes,
He said: O Father, hear me! Let the Fiend
An everlasting monument become
Of sacred justice, which the heavens will view
Rejoicing, and which hell will e'er behold
With shame, with consternation and dismay.
So saying, he drew near to the sepulchre.
Low at the mountain's basis in nocturnal
Obscurity and gloom, among the rocks
And craggy clefts, the silent tombs, are arch'd.
Thick woods and sable gloom the avenue form.
And shelter the sepulchres from the gaze
Of travellers, who, with hasty steps, thence pass.
E'en when the son stands in meridian
Above the turrets of Jerusalem,
A doleful morn with nightly damps and fogs
Is lowering still among the dreary tombs.
There Samma (such was the Demoniac's name)
Exhausted, faint, with misery overwhelm'd,
Lay on his youngest most beloved son's grave.
The Fiend allowed him this short interlapse,
With greater fury soon to torture him,
And on the wretch redoubled rancour vent.
Where in the dost he lay, his elder son
Stood by him and, to heav'n weeping, bemoan'd
The misery of his father, and the loss
Of his so tenderly beloved brother.
The thus lamented child prevailed once
On his affectionate mother, to regard lfl&
His ardent and importunate entreaties:
To take him to his father, whom the rage
Of Satan from society had driv'n,
With anguish dire to roam among the dead.
Ah, my dear Father! said the young belov'd
Benoni, and escaped his mother's arms.
Who terror-stricken hastened after him.
Ah, my dear Father, wilt thou not embrace me?
And, saying so, he fondly -inclining lean'd
Upon his father's hand to press it to his heart.
The father clasps him in his arms, and trembles.
The boy with childhood fondness to him clinging,
The father dashes his head against a rock.
His tender brains reek'd on the gored stone.
The guiltless soul, venting a gentle sigh,
Departed. Now the wretched man bewails,
Disconsolate, his son, and e'er exclaims,
While with his withered arms he clasps the cold
Receptacle of the child's now mouldering bones:
Oh, my Benoni! Oh, my Son Benoni!
He thus exclaims, and tears of sad distress
Gush from his fix'd, now breaking, dying eyes.
Such was the misery of the wretched man,
When the Redeemer tow'rd the tombs advanced.
But Joel, th' elder son, his weeping eyes
Just from his father turning, now beheld
The Saviour, and with glad surprise exclaim'd:
The mighty prophet Jesus, now the bights
Of Olivet descending, hither tends.
Th' Infernal Fiend, on hearing this, cast forth
A lowering glance through th' avenue of the place.
Thus Atheists, that most abject brood, from dark
And vaulted roofs, look forth when sable storms
Ascend the heavens sublime, when 'among dun clouds
The vengeance- dreaded chariots thundering roll.
Till now the Fiend from Samma stood aloof,
Among the rocks, in dark, remote recess,
Thence breathing devilish plagues and torture forth
In slow succession. Bnt now mortify'd,
Smitten and confounded by the Lord's approach
He armed himself with tortures dire of death.
And on the wretched man infuriate burst,
Who bounded in the anguish on his feet,
But void of strength again sank to the ground.
His shattered spirit scarce resisted still
Th' assaults of death; yet, by the Archfiend five
To th' utmost hight of madness, he was climbing
One of the rocks. And in thy sacred presence,
Divine Redeemer, Satan here had dash'd
Him from a pendent far-projecting rock.
But Thou wert there already! Thy divine
And ever -gracious care, on faithful wings
Omnipotent thy hapless creature bore
Unhurt, and saved him from the dire intent.
This galled the Archdestroyer of human kind.
His spirit shook with terror and dismay,
He felt from far of Deity th approach.
Now Jesus turned his healing countenance
On Samma, and his look suffused divine
Restoring power. The wretched man forthwith ttt
Acknowledged and adored the Lord of life.
Into his morbid visage marks of health
Anon returned. He wept aloud to heav'n,
Would speak, but could not utter words for joy
To the Redeemer he op'd wide his arms,
And looked with transport and with eye consol'd
Down from the pendent rock which he had climb'd.
Thus when a pensive soul, with doubts perplexed,
Involved in contemplation, still uncertain,
Despairs of th' endless state of her existence
She. feels a secret tremour, and with dread
Starts shuddering from annihilation back.
But now a kindred sympathizing soul,
(Established in the firm belief of life
Eternal, and relying confident
On promises divine) approaches glad,
And consolation to her friend imparts.
Then the dejected and despairing soul
Revives and soon, with new -imbibed pow'r.
From doubts and sad perplexity extricates,
And is rejoicing in existence now,
Triumphant praising God, as though become
A second time immortal. Even so
The wretched Samma felt that peace of God,
Which is beyond the power of comprehension.
Now the Messiah spake with potent voice
To Satan, saying: Spirit of perdition,
Who art Thou, that e'en in my presence dar'st
Thus to distress and. torture human kind,
Man who, to be redeemed, was preordained?
A sullen growling voice, with wrathful sound,
Reply M: I am the king of th' earth, e'en Satan,
The most exalted deity of the host
Of independent Spirits, from the thrall
Of heaven emancipated, to whom I
Appoint employment more congenial far
To their heroic minds, than the employ
Of heavenly songsters. When thy fame was heard,
And e'en attained the distant gates of hell,
0 mortal Seer! (for Mary will, I wot,
Not bring forth aught immortal!) — I, the prince

And, lo, the gods to me his mother send
Here Portia ceased and turn'd, beckoning, from far,

Portia on leaving her apartments bade,

To Pontius hasten, thus to intimate

Whom heaven forefends and succours! Do not thou

A most tremendous vision from the gods
Hath terrified thy Portia in her sleep!
Calm then, fond Mother, calm thy troubled mind,
And come with, me among the odorous flow'rs,
That, in the morning sun, from noise remote,
I may relate what I was taught this hour.
Now to the silent garden both descended.
The noble Pagan still, with stedfast gaze,
Looked to the ground, and silence still maintain'd,
In wonder and in contemplation wrapp'd,
Reflecting still on her mysterious dream.
Her Angel had presented to her mind
The sacred dream and, with her fervid musings,
Involved still new and more aspiring thoughts,
To touch the finest feelings of her heart,
Still more to move her heavenly-minded soul.
Now extricating from her contemplation,

Great Socrates, — perhaps thou know'st him not;
Hut joy is always thrilling through my breast,
Whenever I give utterance to his name.
A life -most noble and benevolent,
He crowned with a death that threw still more
Transcendent lustre on his virtuous course.
This Socrates, — I ever viewed the Sage
With wonder and, with admiration fond,
Contemplated his virtues so sublime;
Him I beheld before me in a dream.
He stood 'and uttered his immortal name:
I Socrates, whose maxims thou hast eVr
Sincerely honoured, and whose life thou striv'st
To make the pattern of thine earthly course;

Cease at my lore to wonder. The Most High
Is not, what in severer virtue's shade
We deemed and, at the altar, held him forth.
But wholly to devefope to thy view
The awful nature of the Deity,

Of wonder, days in which the most profound
And most sublime event, that e'er the earth

One, greater and far better than myself,
Will nearer guide thee to the sanctuary.
However, this I may to thee impart,
Thus much the candour and simplicity
Of thy ingenuous heart for thee procur'd:
No longer by malignance of the base
Is Socrates oppressed. Elysium
Is fictions. So is the nocturnal stream,
And Minos and the Judges. These were mere
Faint illustrations that from error rose.
Another Judge in judgment doth preside;
And other sans than in Elysium shine,

Behold, the Judge recounts, the balance weighs,
The staff of justice measures every deed
Oh, bow the most exalted virtues, then,

Some are rewarded; most of them are pardon'd.
And thus my heart's ingenuousness obtained

Imperious snd formidable Rome

With this the vision ceased and, vanishing,

I saw them bleed and suffer, but they bore
Their injuries with fortitude of mind,
Men of exalted -virtues, nobler far
Than men around us. Now a tempest rose.

Yet this I may impart to thee, though gladly

The God, then, of a number of the sons

Especially the God of Abraham,

He comprehends what we to fathom fail.

TV exalted prophet Jesus who, by pow'r

I was to bring him forth! his name should be

With weeping eye he, unaverted, gaz'd

What was I? and what am I now! Before.
How wretched and forlorn, how happy now!
This tremour! Oh, this sweet.transporting sense

To what am I transformed? what can he be

Ah more, much morel He is the Son divine
Of the Eternal Father! the divine
Messiah! and his glory? — it transcends
The. glory of an earthly kingdom far!
He is the promised Saviour of the world
But how mysterious his humiliation,
To die — to die on the accursed tree,
And Ob, to rescue me, an heinous sinner!
Bat this I cannot fathom. Yet I know,
He by his power created me anew.
Now, while I am by death subdued, be hath
Invested me with life and endless bliss.
So let me, then, though I cannot comprehend
Thy wondrous nature, ever Thee adore.
Thou art divine, much greater than the greatest
Of Angels; for an Angel could not, thus
Anew create me, and transport my soul
With ecstasy, and lead me to my God.
Such were bis thoughts, and now he sunk absorb'd

The -heavens above, the earth beneath, all smil'd

To one of the attendant Seraphim

O thought of transport! I receiv'd commands,

Canto IX

Evan was returning from the Throne
Of th' awful Judge. Absorbed in thought profound.
On slower wing he passed the temple's bight,
Approached the patriarchal goals, and said:
First join me in devotion. Ere my thoughts
I utter, I must worship. — Silent, all
Prostrated, with profound humility
Adoring the Eternal, th' Infinite
Jehovah. And in silence they arose.
Eloah still stood mute; at last he spake:
0 Thou, Most Holy, whom no name sets forth,
Whose attributes thought cannot comprehend,
Of Beings Thou the First! — To Him I soar'd,
Would face to face behold Him who presides
In judgment, still unreconciled to man,
Encompassed with the gloom of majesty
Terrific, — God! — I had attained the suns,
They were obscured; soared to the pole of heav'n,
There night contended with nocturnal shade;
1 still advanced tow 'id the eternal Throne,
Darkness around me still became more dark,
And still more dark, and now — But I seek names
And find them not, to represent the gloom,
That shrouded the Eternal, find no names
For terrors that were hovering round the Throne.
I stood and heard, amid the silence dread
Of the creation, from afar, the roar
Of floods infernal. Slowly I advanc'd.
Anon, advancing still, the First of th' Angels
Of death exclaim'd: What finite Being dares
Approach this place? — I trembled back, was dumb,
Sunk on my face and, silent, worshipp'd Him
Who sate in judgment. — So th' Immortal spake,
Turned, and enveloped his averted face.
Jesus, his head reclining on his breast,
Appeared as though he slumbered. E'en the rage
Of the blaspheming scoffers now abated.
As th' agitated ocean's turbulence
At last, beneath the sheltering cliff abates.
Those who revered and loved the Son divine,
Disconsolate, roamed round the hill of death,
In it's environs scattered whence, remote,
The Saviour they with weeping eye might see.
Yet all eachother carefully avoid
Lest, by communing, they should still increase
Their sorrow and eachother's feelings wound.
The more especially beloved disciple
And the mother of the awful sufferer,
These only near eachother still remain'd.
They stood before the cross. And the disciple
Who had deny'd, e'en with an oath, that be
Had knowledge of the Saviour, through the sad
And sleepless night and all the morning reared
About alone and, trembling, sought in vain
Alleviation of distress of mind.
Thus on the shore of the relentless sea,
Encompassed by the wreck and floating corpses,
A hapless son still strays' forlorn and mute,
And unaverted views the fearful rock
On which his father perish'd. Now he lifts
His eyes to heaven and, with the bitterness
And anguish keen of self-accusing grief,
Exclaims: My helpless father I forsook!
I rendered him no succour in the hour
Of peril and of dire extremity
I should have rescued him or, in th' attempt,
Have perish'd. — Simon, on an eminence
Near Golgatha now, wholly exhausted, stopp'd,
Too faint to wring his trembling sinking hands.
Ithuriel, bis Guardian, sees his grief,
And in his heart infuses some degree

Though an Immortal. The distressed disciple

Collects himself, as now his eyes to lift,
Looking around, desirous to behold
Some of his friends that he to them might go

But still he stood and viewed Jerusalem.
For, up to Golgatha to look, the mount SO

Unable! Still he laboured to discern
The pompons city. But Jerusalem,
'Though spreading o'er vast fields, though towering high

Her palaces and domes amid the dire

Now tow'rd the sound of voices Simon torrid,

To celebrate the festival, and these
Respecting the Great Prophet's death convers'd,
"Who now was bleeding on the lofty cross.
Simon the bill descended and approach'd
The strangers, hoping in their company
Of the dispersed disciples sonde to find.
But still he found his hopes not realiz'd.

A man of dark complexion, richly' attir'd

But (turning, he saw Simon) here behold

I know thou art a minister of God,

Thou knowest, art his most especial friend,
Ne'er brothers loved' with so.much tenderness,

Ye Friends, all I am able to impart

Kind parent of th' immortal children, ''thou
In quick succession shalt distribute them,
That, in the festal robes of innocence,
And with new names distinguished, they may sing
The Victor, him, who rescued them from death,
And everlasting bliss on them 'bestow'd.
Ye hillocks of the dead, before the hills.
Of all the earth rejoice! Ye mossy graves,
Rejoice before the mountains hoar and huge!
All, slumbering in the silent grave, shall wake.
And thou, O Earth, shalt on the last of days MoS
Come forth effulgent, by th' omnipotence
Of Jesus, whom into thy depths obscure
Thou didst receive, — forth from the awful dust,
Of general judgment, fashioned wholly anew.
The solar beam, and moon's nocturnal light,
Not longer then shall rule thy days and seasons;
Inhabited by righteousness and truth,
The glory of th' Omnipotent, and Christ
Whose blood was flowing on the hill of death,
For ever then shall bo thy glory and light.
So th' earlier martyrs sung, who bore already
The palm of victory, while Stephen yet
Him scarce remotely knew, to whom he was
His testimony with his blood so seal,
The First among the Christian martyr-train.
Yet, Stephen, O how near unto the palm

From thine ordainment till the victor's crown.
Thon saw'st heaven opened, Jesus at the Right

Into the heaven of heavens wast receiv'd.

And they looked up to Jesus with a love,
Too inexpressive for the tongue of man,
And too exalted for the human heart.
To the partakers of the better part, So

Benoni, and Jedidoth, do ye see
His glory? how with gentler beams he deigns,
'The Lord of life and glory, on us to look?

For he created great Eloah too
A finite Spirit; yet, far different is

Such th' infinite perfection of his glory!

And gracious Giver, whom we all adore!
" Adore and love! To every one according

Unto us all the best, the most benign,
The most adorable, to all most lovely!
And (this high soaring, ne'er-explored thought,
Bear you on his distended wings aloft!)
Th' Only begotten of th' Eternal Fathers,
Eternally beloved and loving Son!
Bat here our most exalted faculties

The boundaries, to finite minds prescrib'd.
Angel of God, created long ere we

In transport's unexplored profundity;

W holy in their dole absorbed and languishing

Although he has already approached the. veil
That does conceal the blaze of glory which
Will be unfolded shortly to his view.
The pious women mingled spice and oil,
For the embalming of their heavenly friend,
And tears among the aromatics flow'd:
E'en as the wise attendants of the bridegroom
Were careful to sustain the quivering flame,
That they might meet him when he should appear;
So ye were with solicitude engag'd,
Friends to the Mediator, with the dawn
Of morn to be prepared to hasten to the grave.
Nor did they tarry till the morning dawn'd.
The shades of night had scarcely been dispell'd,
When hence from the disciples they departed.
Some from the cots of Magdala, the spouse WwW

Jesus approached the Throne. Silence became
More silent; now unto the souls the trump
Not longer spake; the Risen Saints stood still:
The Angels still attended, but, not long,
And these too stood, prostrating to adore.
Now Gabriel, no finite being else,
